leads.name: Kauri Pine (City Botanic Gardens)

location.neighbourhood: City Botanic Gardens, south east of the formal flower garden

leads.why_not_verified: National Trust database only (Alice_Street_5): planted 1980, only roughly 45 years old. Too young to be a strong ancient-tree candidate; parked rather than pursued.

leads.name: Anzac (Turkish) Pines (City Botanic Gardens)

location.neighbourhood: City Botanic Gardens, eastern side near the George Street / Parliament House entrance

leads.why_not_verified: Planted 26 April 1979 from seed brought back from Lone Pine, Gallipoli, by veteran soldiers; historically significant (Anzac commemoration) but a group of 5 trees (2 originals plus 3 later replacements after 2 died), each only roughly 46 years old and modest (8m tall). Not pursued this pass: unclear whether it passes the single-collectible-point test given it is a small planted group with a mixed-age replacement history, and the age/size are both slight. Worth a judgement call by a future pass rather than a default no.

leads.name: The Hoop Pine of Ann Hill's Grave (Toowong Cemetery)

location.neighbourhood: Toowong Cemetery (Brisbane General Cemetery), near the grave of Ann Hill, section/grave number not yet found

leads.why_not_verified: Story only, not yet independently confirmed or pinned. Walter Hill, founding superintendent of Brisbane's City Botanic Gardens (the source of most of the city's other published trees), planted a hoop pine beside the grave of his daughter Ann Hill, who died in 1871 aged 21 and was the second person buried at Toowong Cemetery; 'today it is enormous' per a Queensland Stories blog post (roseobrienwriter.blog/2020/07/19/the-first-jacaranda/, found via WebSearch summary only, the live page 403s to WebFetch so this has not been independently read). No exact grave location, no measurements, and no second source found this pass. Toowong Cemetery (Queensland's largest, established 1866, itself on the Queensland Heritage Register id 601773) is a genuinely interesting second Brisbane cluster to research properly in a future pass, given Walter Hill's direct link to the already-published City Botanic Gardens trees, but this lead needs a proper research budget of its own rather than the tail end of a deepen pass. UPDATE 2026-08-29: fetched the Queensland Stories blog post directly (roseobrienwriter.blog/2020/07/19/the-first-jacaranda, previously only seen via search summary) and confirmed its text in full: 'Ann was buried in Toowong Cemetery, only the second person to be buried there; and near her grave, to shade it, Walter planted a hoop pine. Today it is enormous.' A second, independent source (museumofbrisbane.com.au, 'MoB Sunday Stories: the Toowong Cemetery') corroborates that Ann Hill, daughter of Walter Hill, was among the cemetery's earliest burials, but does not mention the hoop pine itself, so the tree-specific claim (planted by Walter Hill to shade the grave) remains single-sourced. Location still cannot be pinned even approximately: Toowong Cemetery is a large heritage cemetery (Queensland Heritage Register id 601773) and Ann Hill's grave is described only as near Governor Blackall's grave 'on the highest knoll' (Blackall was the first burial, grave number 49 per Brisbane City Council's own cemetery map, Ann Hill the second), which is a landmark description rather than a coordinate. Still a lead: needs either a grave/portion number from Brisbane City Council's cemetery records or a photo-located pin.

leads.name: The Hoop Pines of St Paul's Anglican School (Bald Hills)

location.neighbourhood: St Paul's Anglican School, 34 Strathpine Road, Bald Hills

leads.why_not_verified: A pair of hoop pines framing the entrance to the school's Administration Building (a converted 1890s farmhouse), individually listed on the Queensland Heritage Register 22 Feb 2002 (id 602346) and Brisbane's own heritage register (heritage.brisbane.qld.gov.au/heritage-places/220). Believed to mark the site of the original Stewart family farmhouse (Bald Hills' first non-indigenous settlers, 1857); the taller is estimated approximately 190-200 years old (likely remnant old growth pre-dating settlement), the smaller approximately 140-150 years old, per the QHR citation (reproduced near-verbatim on en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoop_Pines,_Bald_Hills, coordinates -27.3151,153.0041 in its infobox) and independently republished with the same age figures by a local news site, albanycreeknews.com.au (fetched directly and read, not just the search summary). Two clearing facts: it is within the ~30 minute day-trip boundary (26 minutes by direct train from Central to Bald Hills station per Rome2Rio), and it is a single collectible point (a pair framing one entrance, not an avenue). NOT delivered because access is unresolved: the trees stand on the grounds of a private independent school (125-acre campus), at the end of the school's main driveway, and no source found this pass states the driveway or entrance is open to the public or visible from Strathpine Road itself. Per the schools rule (only ships with real evidence the grounds are genuinely open), this needs either a source confirming public visibility/access or it stays a lead. Worth a future pass checking satellite/street-level imagery for whether the pines are visible from the road, or contacting the school directly is not an option for a run.

leads.name: Ancient Trees of Indooroopilly Golf Club
leads.species: Multiple: Queensland Blue Gum (Eucalyptus tereticornis), Black She-oak (Allocasuarina littoralis), Spotted Gum (Corymbia citriodora var. variegata), Brushbox (Lophostemon confertus), Small-leaved Fig (Ficus obliqua), Narrow-leaved Ironbark (Eucalyptus crebra), Flooded Gum (Eucalyptus grandis), Moreton Bay Fig (Ficus macrophylla), plus stands of Kauri Pine, Hoop Pine, Bunya Pine and Swamp Cypress

location.neighbourhood: Indooroopilly Golf Club, on the Brisbane River at Indooroopilly, roughly 8km from the CBD

leads.why_not_verified: Found this pass: the club's own natural-history page (indooroopillygolf.com.au/cms/natural-history/original-vegetation-and-ancient-trees, live URL now 404s, read via Wayback snapshot 20230306164028) is an unusually detailed, named, photographed account of 'well over 100 years old' remnant trees across the course, described relative to named golf holes (e.g. a Moreton Bay Fig behind the Blue 1 green, a Flooded Gum between Gold 3 and Gold 4, a Narrow-leaved Ironbark behind the Green 7 tee). This is a real second-source-quality account (the club describing its own land), but two things stop it clearing the bar this pass: (1) no coordinates are given anywhere, only golf-hole-relative descriptions, so nothing can be pinned even approximately without a course map cross-reference; (2) access is genuinely restricted, not merely inconvenient. IGC is a private members' club; only its East course allows paid visitor bookings (contact required, tee time required) and the West course is members-only, and the page itself flags stray-ball hazard ('providing an obstacle for wayward golfers'). Walking the course to look at a tree, as opposed to playing a booked round, is not established as possible, so this does not clear the schools/private-grounds access test. Parked as a lead rather than pursued further; a future pass could try contacting the club's own social media or press coverage for a specific named/measured specimen with a locatable coordinate, or check whether any of the described trees sit close to the club's river frontage where a public riverside path might run.

leads.name: New Farm Park Moreton Bay Fig(s)
leads.why_not_verified: Checked as a possible new cluster point (New Farm Park is a well-known, well-visited public park about 2.5km from the CBD). Tripadvisor reviews and stock-photo captions describe 'the Moreton Bay Fig Tree' as a park highlight with a boardwalk/platform built around it, which suggests either one large specimen or a small grove, not established which this pass. No heritage register listing, no age, no independent written source with real facts was found (Wikipedia's New Farm Park article does not mention fig trees at all; the Queensland Stories 'Brisbane Icons: Fig Trees' post, fetched directly, does not mention New Farm Park either). Parked as a dead end for this pass rather than pursued further; a future pass could try the Brisbane City Council park page or on-the-ground/iNaturalist photos to establish whether it is one tree or several and find a second source.

blocked.name: Weeping Fig Avenue (City Botanic Gardens, eastern river path)

location.neighbourhood: City Botanic Gardens, eastern river path from the Edward Street entrance

blocked.reason: National Trust database (Alice_Street_13) explicitly describes this as an 'Avenue' of 9 trees planted by head gardener James Pink (1881-1886) along the riverbank, distinct from the already-published pair at the Alice Street gate (bne_009, a different National Trust entry, 147_Alice_Street_6). Not a single collectible point, same reasoning as the already-blocked Bunya Pine Avenue; never ship as one entry.

blocked.name: Bunya Pine Avenue (City Botanic Gardens)
blocked.reason: Not a single collectible point. Row of roughly 18 mature Bunya Pines planted by Walter Hill 1858-1867, skirting several hundred metres of the eastern river walk from inside the Edward Street entrance. Well documented (National Trust database: trusttrees.org.au/tree/QLD/Brisbane/Brisbane_City_Botanic_Gardens_Alice_Street_8; State Library of Queensland blog; Wikipedia calls it explicitly 'an avenue of bunya pines') but per the verify-pass rule an avenue is blocked regardless of fame or documentation quality. If a single standout specimen within the row is ever individually distinguished by a source (e.g. the largest or first-planted), it could be lifted out as its own entry.

Not a single collectible point, same reasoning as the already-blocked Bunya Pine Avenue and Weeping Fig Avenue; never ship as one entry. If a single standout specimen within one of the three groupings is ever individually distinguished by a source, it could be lifted out as its own entry.

note:
Brisbane City Council's 558-record significant/landscape tree overlay (data/registers/brisbane-significant-landscape-trees.json) carries NO species, name, age or vitality field, only a designation polygon centroid; it does not by itself clear the two-source bar for any tree and none of it was directly usable this pass without a named tree to match it to. Checked distance from each of the 8 verified City Botanic Gardens/Eagle Street trees to the nearest of the 558 overlay points: nearest was 520m (Eagle Street Fig Trees) and 535-745m for the Botanic Gardens trees, i.e. none of the overlay's individually-designated points sit close enough to plausibly be the same tree, so the overlay was not cited as a source for any of the 8. A future pass with more time could try to match named significant trees elsewhere in Brisbane (New Farm Park, Roma Street Parkland, Mount Coot-tha Botanic Gardens, university campuses) against the overlay's remaining ~550 unmatched points to grow a second cluster; this pass stayed inside the single City Botanic Gardens / Eagle Street cluster (max pairwise distance 1.12km) per the brief's preference for a dense walkable cluster over scattered candidates.

(3) New ground checked: Kangaroo Point (BCC's own Natural History Trail page names no individual tree, only general planting/heritage note), Milton's Haig Road Fig Tree turned up again independently via heritage.brisbane.qld.gov.au/heritage-places/1027 and confirmed as the SAME tree already published as bne_020, not a new candidate. Indooroopilly Golf Club's own detailed 'Original Vegetation and Ancient Trees' page (new find, added to leads above) is the most substantive material found this pass, real named/photographed ancient trees over 100 years old, but has no coordinates and sits on a private members' club course with only paid, booked, visitor golf access (not casual walking access), so it does not clear hard rule 10 or the pinnability bar this pass. Conclusion consistent with all five prior deepen attempts: the 558-point significant-landscape-tree overlay remains unusable without names, and Brisbane's remaining named heritage trees outside the existing City Botanic Gardens/Newstead/Toowong clusters are either avenues (blocked), too young, unpinnable, or access-restricted. Recommend this city wait for a reader submission or a genuinely new source (e.g. a council press release, a new Queensland Heritage Register listing) rather than a sixth from-zero web sweep of the same ground.
